item.title: @piyush1304kumar commented on "Rule about third-party code is changing"
item.description:
hello I confirm that my code is 100% my own work, written during the contest, and is not copied from any other participant. I based my approach on the standard two-pointer subsequence template which has been public for years—long before Codeforces Round 2106.Public source (LeetCode 392 “Is Subsequence”, cached Feb 1 2024): https://web.archive.org/web/20240201000000/https://leetcode.com/problems/is-subsequence/solutions/In that article you’ll find this canonical loop: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ //this is code int i = 0, j = 0; while (i < s.size() && j < t.size()) { if (s[i] == t[j]) i++; j++; } return i == s.size(); ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ I used the exact same idea of advancing a pointer j over the “big” array a[], and advancing i over the “small” array b[] only when a match is found.How my code differs from the LeetCode snippet, and from the other submission Variable names and data structures
In my solution I call the input arrays vector<int> a, b; and my two pointer indices are int j (over a) and loop index i (over b).
I wrap the logic into pref[] and suf[] arrays of size m+2 to record where each prefix/suffix match ends, then combine them.
I use inf = n+1 and ans = 1e18 as sentinels.
The other submission uses f[], g[], variables named pos instead of j, and LLONG_MAX instead of 1e18.
Extension to suffix‐pass
LeetCode’s template only checks “Is b a subsequence of a?”
My code runs two passes: a left‐to‐right to fill pref[i], and a right‐to‐left to fill suf[i]. That combination is my original idea for this problem.
Control flow and output logic
I check if (pref[m] <= n) cout<<0; then otherwise compute ans = min(b[i]) over valid split points—none of which appears in the LeetCode article.All of this code was written in my local editor during the contest on April 24 2025. I only used the two-pointer subsequence search as a starting template (publicly available long before the contest, see cached link above). I did not copy from any other competitor. Please check the cached page and my variable names; you will see the clear lineage from a generic tutorial to my extended solution.</int>

item.title: @prvocislo commented on "IOI Preperation"
item.description: Congratulations!In general, in IOI, strategy matters a lot more than on CodeForces. You should do a lot of IOI-style virtual contests to get used to it and find a strategy that works the best for you. Upsolving is also important — try to upsolve all the problems relevant for your desired medal, so for example, if you're aiming for silver, you should upsolve all the problems with 50+ solves. When upsolving, try to solve as many subtasks as you can on your own (it is important to be able to solve and implement subtasks fast so that you don't miss any obvious points) and then read the editorial and try to code the rest. You can use oi-checklist to track your progress. This is how I trained for IOI.As you've mentioned, modern IOI problems are a bit different than the old ones. I'd say IOI problems from 2015+ are the most relevant ones to train on. After you solve most of them, you can move on to other olympiads, and the older editions of IOI. JOI problems are also great to train on, but I wouldn't recommend starting with them, as they are quite hard, which could be demotivating.
